title: Social Media Creates an Echo Chamber for Leaders
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Recommendation algorithms are the subject here, and the argument is about what they do to a person's capacity to encounter an unfamiliar idea. The author begins with the mechanism in plain terms — the feed guarantees more of whatever you have already found — and illustrates it with deliberately trivial interests, from professional wrestling to flower arrangements to gameshow trivia, to make the point that the machinery is indifferent to subject matter. The effect is described as amplification of existing preference and bias until whatever you already thought is underlined and highlighted repeatedly, which makes genuine contact with dissenting views difficult. The second half applies this to leaders, who are said to inhabit their own echo chamber of settled views about business, strategy, innovation and tactics, and who often do not recognise that seeing leadership through a different lens is work. Older, non-algorithmic media — books, magazines, podcasts, keynotes, daily emails — are defended on exactly this ground: they surface ideas not currently on the reader's radar and briefly suspend the influence of the feed. The closing warning is that a leader whose information diet is built from their own clicks will simply never meet the ideas they most need.
points: The author's framing is that the harm is not false content but narrowed exposure: the feed reaffirms whatever bias a person brings to their search for insight.

Trivial examples are chosen on purpose — wrestling, flower arranging, hip-hop, experimental medical procedures — to show the mechanism operates identically regardless of how consequential the interest is.
Leaders are argued to be especially vulnerable because their echo chamber is professional rather than recreational, covering strategy and innovation, and therefore looks like legitimate learning.
Curated, editorially chosen media are defended as a corrective precisely because the reader did not select the topic — encountering a new author sends the algorithms to the curb for a moment.
Seeing leadership through a different lens is described as a climb that many leaders do not recognise they need to make, which makes the problem self-concealing.
quotes: The algorithms of social media ensure you will always find more of what you have already found on the internet.
If you are captivated by professional wrestling, flower arrangements, or hip-hop, it feeds you streams of images, videos, photos, and text that encourage those passions.
What shows up on your phone is an echo chamber of like-minded content and viewpoints.
They live in their own echo chamber of similar thoughts about business, strategy, innovation, and tactics.
That’s why podcasts, keynote speeches, books, magazines, and daily emails are so important. They encourage us to think about ideas and issues not currently on our radar.
Leaders who are addicted to the daily feed of information based upon their own clicks stand a chance of missing many good ideas and learnings.
